todays_goal: Launch Grade 6 homeschool, establish routines, and gather baseline evidence without treating unfamiliar Grade 6 content as failure.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: Completed Grade 5 mathematics at Fort Worth Country Day; prior records show strong math performance, but the diagnostic is intended to identify what has actually been taught and retained.
lessons.course_context: This baseline samples several Grade 6 domains so later lessons can begin at the correct point. It is not a report-card grade.
learning_objectives: Show current fluency with fractions and decimals.
Identify Grade 6 topics not yet learned.
Provide evidence for pacing decisions.
lessons.why_it_matters: A diagnostic prevents the course from wasting time on secure skills or rushing past skills that still need direct teaching.

vocabulary.definition: A check used to find what you already know and what still needs teaching.
A fraction made by switching numerator and denominator.
A rate that compares a quantity to 1 unit.

lessons.written_instruction: Complete core questions first. Show enough work to make reasoning visible. If a topic has not been learned, write NOT LEARNED YET and continue. Do not interpret unfamiliar algebra, ratios, percent, geometry, data, or probability as failure.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the Day 1 Grade 6 mathematics diagnostic in the printed packet.

exit_ticket.prompt: Name one math skill that felt secure and one topic that felt unfamiliar.
exit_ticket.answer: Any accurate self-assessment supported by the diagnostic.
exit_ticket.rubric: Names one secure skill and one unfamiliar topic honestly.

lessons.voice_prompt: Explain that this is a baseline, not a grade. Remind Atticus to write NOT LEARNED YET for unfamiliar topics. Do not teach answers during the diagnostic; clarify directions only.
lessons.teacher_notes: Later review showed strong decimal subtraction and some fraction work, but major Grade 6 domains had not yet been taught. Future lessons must teach before testing.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: Close reading baseline: The Lantern Test
lessons.previous_learning: Grade 5 humanities and independent reading experience.
lessons.course_context: The opening reading unit establishes careful reading, inference, vocabulary in context, theme, summary, and evidence habits.
learning_objectives: Answer literal and inferential questions from a Grade 6 story.
Use text details to support an answer.
Distinguish theme from a one-word topic.
lessons.why_it_matters: Reading closely and supporting ideas with evidence transfers to every academic subject.

vocabulary.definition: A complete message about life or people developed by a story.
A specific detail from the text that supports an idea.

lessons.written_instruction: Read The Lantern Test slowly. Answer every part. For questions asking what a detail means or why it matters, explain what it reveals, not only what happened.

worked_examples.title: Topic vs theme
worked_examples.problem: A character keeps improving after mistakes.
worked_examples.solution: Topic: failure. Theme: People can improve when they study mistakes instead of hiding them.
worked_examples.explanation: A theme is a complete transferable statement.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the Day 1 close-reading questions and objective summary.

exit_ticket.prompt: State one theme of The Lantern Test as a complete sentence.
exit_ticket.answer: A supported theme such as: Careful testing and learning from failure can produce better solutions.
exit_ticket.rubric: Complete transferable message supported by the story.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not tell Atticus the theme. Clarify vocabulary if asked, then use questions such as 'What does that detail show?' to push from literal understanding to significance.
lessons.teacher_notes: Day 1 work showed comprehension stronger than response precision. Methodical, theme, significance, and complete CER responses became explicit teaching targets.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.course_context: A first-day sample establishes a baseline for organization, sentence control, stamina, detail, and conventions.
learning_objectives: Plan and draft a 400-600 word response.
Revise for clarity and conventions.
Preserve the original draft as baseline evidence.
lessons.why_it_matters: A baseline lets teacher and student measure real writing growth over the year.

vocabulary.definition: A version of writing that can still be improved.
Changing ideas, organization, or wording to make writing clearer and stronger.

lessons.written_instruction: Write independently about an experience that changed the way you thought about something. Plan briefly, draft, then revise. Do not use AI to compose the piece.

worked_examples.title: Specific detail
worked_examples.solution: Stronger: After the first experiment failed, I changed one variable and finally saw why the result was different.
worked_examples.explanation: Specific actions and details make writing clearer.

independent_practice.prompt: Write the 400-600 word baseline response from the packet.

exit_ticket.prompt: Circle one sentence you revised and explain what you improved.
exit_ticket.answer: Any accurate explanation of a revision.
exit_ticket.rubric: Identifies a real revision and its purpose.

lessons.voice_prompt: Help only with understanding the prompt and planning. Do not compose sentences for the baseline sample.
lessons.teacher_notes: Baseline is preserved for later comparison.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.course_context: This begins the Light and Matter unit through observation, modeling, and evidence.
learning_objectives: Observe transmission, reflection, and absorption.
Record evidence in a table.
Draw a simple light-path model.
lessons.why_it_matters: Understanding light interactions explains visibility, mirrors, windows, color, and later optical systems.

vocabulary.definition: To bounce light from a surface.
To take in light energy rather than pass or reflect most of it.

lessons.written_instruction: Test household materials with a flashlight from a consistent distance. Record what happens and draw arrows showing a light path.

worked_examples.title: Mirror
worked_examples.problem: What happens when light hits a mirror?
worked_examples.explanation: Much of the light changes direction at the reflective surface.

guided_practice.prompt: Predict whether clear plastic mainly transmits, reflects, or absorbs visible light.
guided_practice.hint: Can you normally see through it?

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the material test table and draw one light-path model.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain how light can travel from a flashlight to a wall after interacting with a material.
exit_ticket.answer: A correct path such as source -> material -> reflected/transmitted light -> wall.
exit_ticket.rubric: Uses arrows/direction and identifies the interaction.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach the three interaction terms before asking for conclusions. Ask what was actually observed before discussing why it happened.
lessons.teacher_notes: Later work showed useful light-path reasoning; vocabulary classification required refinement.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: Elementary world and United States geography.
lessons.course_context: The course begins with map literacy before Ancient Greece.
learning_objectives: Locate major world regions and reference lines.
Use latitude and longitude vocabulary accurately.
Identify gaps for later instruction.
lessons.why_it_matters: Historical events make more sense when the student can picture where they occurred.

vocabulary.definition: Imaginary east-west lines measuring distance north or south of the Equator.
Imaginary north-south lines measuring distance east or west of the Prime Meridian.

lessons.written_instruction: Label the requested world locations on a blank map without coaching. Then review latitude and longitude.

worked_examples.title: Latitude
worked_examples.explanation: The Equator is the reference line for north/south latitude.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the world-map baseline and coordinate questions in the packet.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain the difference between latitude and longitude.
exit_ticket.answer: Latitude measures north/south position; longitude measures east/west position.

lessons.voice_prompt: Clarify map vocabulary but do not supply locations during the baseline portion.
lessons.teacher_notes: Baseline only; later Ancient Greece work supplies stronger geography reasoning evidence.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: Several years of French at Fort Worth Country Day.
lessons.course_context: French continues from prior study; it is not beginner Spanish or a restart from greetings only.
learning_objectives: Use familiar French in a short oral exchange.
Show retained present-tense vocabulary and grammar.
Identify areas needing review.
lessons.why_it_matters: A continuing-language baseline preserves prior learning and avoids unnecessary restart.

vocabulary.definition: Change a verb form to match the subject and tense.
A verb form used for what happens now or regularly.

lessons.written_instruction: Respond orally and in writing using familiar French. If a structure is forgotten, mark it for review rather than switching subjects/languages.

worked_examples.title: Simple introduction
worked_examples.problem: Introduce yourself and state a preference.
worked_examples.solution: Je m'appelle Atticus. J'aime la musique.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the continuing French baseline in the packet and a short oral conversation.

exit_ticket.prompt: Say two complete French sentences about yourself.
exit_ticket.answer: Any two grammatically reasonable sentences using known language.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use natural French pronunciation. Treat Atticus as a continuing French learner and reduce English support when he understands.
lessons.teacher_notes: Prior school records support continuing French placement.

lessons.subject: computer_science
lessons.course_context: The opening unit builds system thinking before algorithms, conditionals, variables, data, and AI.
learning_objectives: Classify inputs and outputs in familiar systems.
Describe processing at a high level.
Recognize that AI systems also receive inputs and produce outputs.
lessons.why_it_matters: Understanding systems makes later programming and AI concepts easier to reason about.

vocabulary.definition: Information or a signal given to a system.
The steps a system uses to transform input into output.

lessons.written_instruction: Classify familiar devices and services by input, processing, storage, and output. Focus on system behavior rather than hidden technical details.

worked_examples.title: Camera
worked_examples.solution: Input: light/image information. Output: a digital image.
worked_examples.explanation: The device processes sensor data into an image.

guided_practice.prompt: Identify one input and one output for a voice assistant.
guided_practice.hint: Think about what the user gives it and what it returns.

independent_practice.prompt: Classify the systems listed in the Day 1 packet.

exit_ticket.prompt: In one sentence, explain input -> processing -> output using a device of your choice.
exit_ticket.rubric: Names a plausible input, transformation/process, and output.

lessons.voice_prompt: Use ordinary devices and systems as examples. Avoid unnecessary jargon; define each technical term when first used.
lessons.teacher_notes: Foundation lesson before algorithms and conditionals.

lessons.subject: pe
lessons.course_context: Initial movement benchmark; later PE is not required in every packet.
learning_objectives: Complete a safe warm-up and skill session.
Record one baseline benchmark.
lessons.why_it_matters: A baseline helps measure improvement rather than compare to others.

vocabulary.definition: A starting measurement used for later comparison.

lessons.written_instruction: Complete warm-up, ball mastery, movement, and a juggling benchmark safely.

independent_practice.prompt: Complete the movement session and record your benchmark.

exit_ticket.prompt: Record one benchmark and one technique goal.
exit_ticket.rubric: Includes a measurable benchmark and a technique goal.

lessons.voice_prompt: Prioritize safety, technique, and measurable personal improvement.
lessons.teacher_notes: PE included on Day 1; later days may omit PE based on schedule.
